title: Going home
hook: at Sikh funerals the bedtime prayer Kirtan Sohila is sung, and death is spoken of as going home (Guru Granth Sahib 12–13)

segments.voice: Yesterday, a grave and the Prophet's advice: visit them, because they remind us. Did you read a name on a stone? Today, new voices: Sikh hymns sung at bedtime, and at the very end. Day seven hundred eighty-six.

Night, in a Sikh home. The lights are low, the day's noise is over, and before sleep someone reads a short set of hymns from the Guru Granth Sahib. They're called Kirtan Sohila, and they're meant for the end of the day. Now a different scene. A cremation. The family has gathered, the fire has been lit, and the same hymns are sung. The words that close an ordinary evening also close a life. Some readers hear in that a single thought: sleep and death are both a kind of going home.
screen: `A BEDTIME PRAYER.` → `THE SAME HYMNS AT A CREMATION.` → `SLEEP AND DEATH, BOTH HOMEWARD.`

segments.voice: First, a night prayer. The Sikh code of conduct, the Rehat Maryada, names Kirtan Sohila as the prayer to recite before sleeping. It also says that at a cremation, once the pyre is lit, Kirtan Sohila is recited and the Ardas, the Sikh prayer of petition, is offered. Second, a wedding. The first hymn, by Guru Nanak, doesn't sound like a funeral at all. It sounds like a wedding. The soul is pictured as a bride. The date of her wedding has already been written. Her friends are told to gather and pour oil on the threshold, a wedding custom, and to bless her so she may meet her Lord. In this picture, death isn't a thief at the door. It's the groom's party arriving. Third, the summons. The hymn goes on: the call goes out to every home, every day. Remember the One who calls. The day is coming. It's said gently, the way a mother reminds a child that the bus will come in the morning. Fourth, going home. Sikh teaching speaks of death as the soul returning to the One it came from, and accepting it as God's will. The Rehat Maryada asks mourners not to wail or beat their breasts, but to turn to the hymns instead. Grief is not forbidden. It's given a song. Some readers hear the nightly singing as a small rehearsal for the night that ends everything, and the singing at a cremation as tucking someone in. Going home.
screen: `A PRAYER BEFORE SLEEP.` · `THE SOUL AS A BRIDE.` · `THE CALL REACHES EVERY HOME.` · `GRIEF IS GIVEN A SONG.` · then, large: `GOING HOME.`

segments.voice: Today's practice belongs to dusk, but any hour will do. Sit comfortably and let the shoulders drop. Then hum something quietly. Any tune you know well and find gentle: a lullaby, a hymn, a song from home. Keep it low and soft, barely more than breath. Feel the hum in the chest and the face. Let it be the sound of a day closing, of a door being shut gently for the night. If you know a line of Sohila, or a prayer of your own tradition, you can hum or say that instead. The bell holds the time.
Going home: how the Sikh bedtime hymns, Kirtan Sohila, sung each night and at cremations, picture death: a bride's wedding, a call to every home, a soul returning. Today's word.
Your line: tucking someone in. Tonight, before sleep, close the day on purpose, with a hum, a prayer, or one quiet breath at the door. Day seven hundred eighty-six.

howItsDone: Sikhs recite Kirtan Sohila before sleep each night, and at a cremation it is recited after the pyre is lit, followed by the Ardas; mourners are asked to sing hymns rather than wail.

original.note: Gurmukhi, from the Guru Granth Sahib: the Sikh bedtime hymns, also sung at cremations.

trapdoor: what you thought: a sad song for funerals.
what it means: bedtime hymns that picture death as a wedding and a going home.
what a scholar hears: Guru Nanak's opening hymn uses the bride's wedding day and the daily summons to every home.

sources.ref: Sikh Rehat Maryada: bedtime prayer; funeral ceremonies

notes: Kirtan Sohila paraphrased (no Macauliffe quotation). Confirm the first shabad's images: the wedding date written, friends pouring oil on the threshold, blessing the bride to meet her Lord, the summons sent to every home every day, remembering the One who calls, the day drawing near.
'Oil on the threshold, a wedding custom': confirm the description.
Rehat Maryada: confirm (a) Kirtan Sohila before sleep, (b) recited at the cremation after the pyre is lit, followed by Ardas, (c) mourners asked not to wail or beat breasts.
'Sikh teaching speaks of death as the soul returning to the One it came from, and accepting it as God's will' (hukam / bhana) is a summary; confirm wording.
'Like a mother reminding a child about the bus' and 'tucking someone in' are images of our own, not claims about the text; confirm tone.
Original: confirm Gurmukhi spelling ਕੀਰਤਨ ਸੋਹਿਲਾ and transliteration.
